title: The Seduction of Pessimism
supportedClaims: Pessimism feels sophisticated because danger is vivid, immediate, and emotionally legible, while progress is slow and easy to overlook.
The mind notices crashes, frauds, and losses faster than it notices decades of compounding improvement, so bad news gets mistaken for deeper truth.
The practical lesson is to pair realism about fragility with long-run optimism about adaptation, progress, and human problem-solving.
caution: Optimism that ignores ruin is naive, but pessimism that ignores progress can be just as distorting and often more expensive.
